content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"Across all three blind responses the settled view is that a 'name' symbolizes the bearer's essential identity, character, reputation, authority, and presence — supremely the name of God/Jesus, which is virtually equivalent to the person himself. Recognized facets include delegated authority ('in the name'), reputation/renown, Name-theology (God's name dwelling in the sanctuary), naming as dominion, new-name transformation, and covenant ownership/belonging.","book_summary":"The book defines the Name as the covenant identity of a house, concretely constituted by three things appointed by its Head: the Word (the manna), the covenant law (the stone tables), and the fruitful priesthood (Aaron's budded rod) — i.e., the contents of the ark within the house built 'for the name.' A counterfeit Name substitutes a different word, covenant, or priesthood; the Name is 'taken in vain' when any of the three is rejected, replaced, or removed; a bride takes her Husband's Name by entering His house, coming under His authority, and obeying Him.","consensus_core_identification":"Name = the person himself: his revealed character, identity, authority, presence, and reputation.","book_core_identification":"Name = the covenant identity of a house, defined by three appointed constituents (word, covenant law, priesthood) housed in the ark; taken by entering the house and submitting to its Head.","core_relation":"COMPATIBLE_OVERLAP","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book retains the consensus category (name as covenant identity and authority of the one who bears/heads it) but converts an abstract personal-character symbol into a precise tripartite structural definition tied to the ark's contents. This reclassifies key cases: Exodus 20:7 ('taking the name in vain') is moved from irreverent or dishonest use of God's name (the consensus reading) to corporate apostasy — rejecting or replacing the appointed word, covenant, or priesthood. It also introduces the category of a 'counterfeit Name' (substituted word/covenant/priesthood), which no consensus response admits, and it institutionalizes 'name = presence in the house' (echoing Name-theology, Deut 12 / 1 Kgs 8) into a checklist of three constituents. Cases the consensus centers on — name as personal character (Ex 34:5-7), reputation (Prov 22:1), phonetic/verbal invocation — are demoted or excluded from the definition.","material_contradiction":"No outright contradiction of the central referent: the book still treats the Name as identity and as authority one comes under (the bride taking her Husband's Name aligns with consensus 'covenant ownership/belonging' and 'delegated authority' facets). The sharpest tension is over Exodus 20:7, where the book's reading (vain = removing one of the three constituents) displaces, but does not strictly negate, the standard reading about misuse of the name.","rationale":"Both readings agree that a name is far more than a label and signifies covenant identity and authority. The book does not replace the referent — it remains identity conferred by and binding one to the Head — but it materially changes the definition's precision and conditions: identity is corporate (a house, not primarily a person's character) and is exhaustively specified as word + covenant + priesthood, derived from Heb 9:4's ark contents inside the house built 'for the name' (2 Sam 7:13; 1 Kgs 8:20-21). This adds cases (counterfeit names, priesthood-removal as name-violation) and reclassifies others (the third commandment). That is genuine boundary disagreement within the same general category, fitting REFINED rather than DIVERGENT (no replaced referent) or NOVEL (identity/authority/Name-dwelling-in-the-house are all recognized consensus facets, especially Response A's Name-theology alternative).","citation_support":"PARTIAL","strongest_objection":"One could argue DIVERGENT: the consensus says the name IS the person (his character and presence), while the book says the Name IS three objects/institutions appointed within a house — a different kind of referent — and its reading of Exodus 20:7 effectively rejects the universal understanding of that commandment. If the shift from 'person's character' to 'house's appointed contents' is judged a replacement of the referent rather than a re-specification of covenant identity, the verdict would be DIVERGENT. The citations, moreover, never state the equation name = manna + tables + rod; it is built by inference across Heb 9:4, Deut 8:3, Deut 4:13, and Num 17, so a critic could rate support INSUFFICIENT rather than PARTIAL.","confidence":"medium"}
